slides.title: Small Molecule Drugs
text: • Low molecular weights, typicall less than 900 Daltons
• Typically administered orally, but can also be given intravenously or via other routes
• Often designed to interact with specific molecular targets (e.g., enzymes, receptors)
• Capable of diffusing across cell membranes

slides.title: Small Molecule Drugs
text: • Generally easier and cheaper to manufacture.
• Can be stored and distributed more easily.
• May cause off-target effects and toxicity.
• Often subject to drug resistance (e.g., antibiotics).

slides.title: Biologics
text: • Large, complex molecules derived from living cells,
• Typically administered via injection or infusion (due to poor oral bioavailability)
• Highly specific to biological targets (e.g., receptors, signaling molecules).
• Monoclonal antibodies (Herceptin for breast cancer), insulin (diab etes), vaccines.

slides.title: Biologics
text: • Reduced risk of off-target effects compared to small molecules.
• Effective for conditions that small molecules cannot target

slides.title: Pharmacokinetics (PK)
text: • What the body does to drugs

slides.title: Absorption
text: • Movement of the drug from the site of administration
• pH and blood flow at the absorption site
• Influcences bioavailability (how much drug reaches systemic circulation)

slides.title: Distribution
text: • Dispersion of the drug through the body’s tissues and fluids.
• Blood flow to tissues and organs
• Drug binding to plasma proteins (e.g., albumin)
• Ability to cross biological barriers (e.g., blood-brain barrier)
• Volume of distribution: a measure of
how extensively a drug spreads in the body.

slides.title: Metabolism
text: • Chemical transformation of the drug, mainly in the liver
• Phase 1: Modification (e.g., oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) by enzymes (e.g., cytochrome P450)
• Phase 2: Conjugation (e.g., glucuronidation) to make drugs more water-soluble.

slides.title: Excretion
text: • Elimination of drugs and their metabolites from the body
• Half-life: Time required for the drug concentration to reduce by 50%.

slides.title: Pharmadynamics (PD)
text: • What drugs do to the body

text: • Dose-response curve: Relationship between drug dose and the
• ED50: Dose that produces 50% of the maximum effect
• Emax: Maximum effect a drug can produce

• Sensitization: Increased response to a drug after repeated use.

slides.title: What is Material Science?

and processing of materials (metals, ceramics, polymers, etc.)
• Key challenges include designing new materials with targeted properties
(for energy, electronics, etc.) and scaling up from lab to industry
• Applications to semiconductors, batteries, biomaterials, and more

slides.title: Categorization by Electronic Properties
text: Have free electrons that allow easy charge flow. No band gap.
No free carriers under normal conditions. Large band gap.
Conductivity can be tuned by doping or temperature. Moderate band gap.
• Band gap is the energy difference (in electronvolts, eV) between:
• The top of the valence band (highest energy electrons bound to atoms)
• The bottom of the conduction band (lowest energy electrons that can move freely)
• Conceptually similar to HOMO-LUMO gap for molecules (non-materials)

slides.title: Categorization by Optical Properties
text: • Occurs when a material does not absorb visible light.
• Requires a wide band gap, so photons pass through without excitation (e.g., glass, quartz).
• Emission of light from a material after absorbing energy.
